mcqs.question: A Shape type is defined as exactly one of Circle, Rectangle, or Triangle. What kind of algebraic data type is Shape?
options: A product type, because every Shape has fields describing its dimensions
Neither — Shape is just an interface, not an algebraic data type
A hybrid type that is both sum and product simultaneously with no distinction
A sum type, because a Shape value is exactly one of several distinct variants, never more than one
mcqs.explanation: Shape being 'exactly one of several variants' is the definition of a sum type (OR); each variant may itself be a product type internally (e.g. Circle holding a radius field), but that doesn't make Shape itself a product. It isn't merely an interface, and sum and product are distinct, composable concepts, not an undifferentiated hybrid.

mcqs.question: A function currently returns a value of type T and throws an exception on failure. What does rewriting it to return Result<T, E> change about error handling?
options: It makes the function run faster because exceptions are no longer thrown
It has no real effect — Result<T, E> is just a renamed exception
The failure path becomes part of the return type itself, so a caller can't get the success value without acknowledging the possibility of an error
It removes the need to handle errors at all, since Result always resolves to a value
mcqs.explanation: Result<T, E> encodes both outcomes in the type signature, so unwrapping a value forces the caller to confront the Err case — unlike a thrown exception, which a caller can simply forget to catch. It's not primarily a performance change, it's a genuinely different mechanism from exceptions, and it doesn't eliminate the need to handle errors — it makes forgetting to handle them a compile-time issue instead of a runtime one.

mcqs.question: In the Kotlin sealed-class example, what happens if a developer adds a new Triangle-like subtype of Shape but forgets to add a branch for it in an existing when expression over Shape?
options: The when expression silently returns null for the missing case
Nothing changes until the new type is actually passed in at runtime, then it throws
The compiler refuses to compile that when expression, since sealed classes enable exhaustiveness checking
Kotlin automatically generates a default branch that returns 0.0
mcqs.explanation: Because Shape is sealed, the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes and enforces that every when expression over it handles all of them — a missing case is a compile-time error, not a runtime surprise. Kotlin doesn't auto-generate a fallback branch, silently return null, or defer the failure to runtime for a sealed hierarchy.

mcqs.question: Calling .map(str.upper) on an Option<str> that holds None does what?
options: Throws an error because there's no string to call upper on
Calls str.upper on the string "None" and wraps that result
Returns None without ever calling str.upper — map only applies the function when a value is present
Converts the None into Some("") and then applies str.upper to the empty string
mcqs.explanation: map on a sum type like Option applies the wrapped function only in the case where a value is actually present, passing through the empty case unchanged and never invoking the function at all. It doesn't throw, doesn't invent a placeholder string, and doesn't convert None into a present value.

mcqs.question: An order is modeled with isPaid: bool, paymentDate: Date?, and isRefunded: bool as separate fields. What's the core problem this design has that a PaymentStatus sum type avoids?
options: It uses too much memory compared to a sum type
It's slower to check than a pattern match
It's impossible to add a fourth status later with either design
The fields can be set to combinations that don't correspond to any real, valid order state, like isPaid=false with a paymentDate set
mcqs.explanation: The independent boolean/nullable fields can be combined into states that make no business sense, because nothing ties them together — the type doesn't encode the actual relationship. A sum type's variants are the only constructible states, so illegal combinations simply have no constructor. Memory and speed aren't the core issue here, and both designs can in fact be extended with a new state later.

mcqs.question: You're modeling a value that always has the same three fields present, with no branching identity between different kinds of it. Which type should you reach for?
options: A sum type with a single variant, to leave room for future cases
A plain product type (a struct or record) — a sum type would add ceremony without modeling anything real
A sum type with one variant per possible field combination
An Option<T> wrapping the whole structure
mcqs.explanation: When data is uniformly present with no distinct identity to branch on, a sum type has nothing real to represent — it's the wrong tool, and a plain product type is simpler and equally correct. A single-variant sum type, an Option wrapper, or enumerating field combinations as variants all add complexity without modeling an actual choice.
